'''White sage''' (''Salvia apiana'') is a Californian coastal-sage-scrub shrub, sacred to the Chumash, Cahuilla, Kumeyaay and other Indigenous peoples of southern California, for whom it is a ceremonial and medicinal plant.

== Chemistry ==

The leaf oil is dominated by '''1,8-cineole''' (eucalyptol) and '''camphor''', with α-pinene, β-pinene and camphene — antimicrobial, and the reason the smoke has a documented effect on airborne bacterial counts rather than a merely symbolic one. It also carries diterpenoids of the ''Salvia'' type. It contains '''no thujone''' in the quantities that make ''Salvia officinalis'' and wormwood a concern, and it is '''not''' ''Salvia divinorum'' — an unrelated Mexican species with entirely different pharmacology.

== Conservation, and why this entry is mostly about sourcing ==

'''White sage is under real pressure from commercial harvest.''' Demand from the wellness market has driven large-scale poaching from public and tribal land in southern California, documented in repeated law-enforcement seizures. Indigenous communities from whom the practice was taken have asked, publicly and repeatedly, that non-Native buyers stop purchasing wild-harvested white sage.

The practical consequences for anyone sourcing it:

* '''Cultivated''' white sage is available, grows readily, and is the only defensible commercial source. It is easy to grow from seed or cutting in Mediterranean climates.
* '''Wild-harvested''' bundles at wellness retail should be assumed to be of unverifiable provenance.
* Other aromatic plants — including [[Imphepho]], which carries its own living tradition and is cultivated and traded by the communities who use it — serve the same practical purpose without the same problem.

In the Institute's inventory white sage is marked '''"to be sourced — wild collection pending; consider cultivated sources"'''. On the record above, cultivated is the answer, and the entry is kept largely to say so.

== Cautions ==

Any smoke is a respiratory irritant, and matters in asthma. Camphor and cineole are toxic in concentrated essential-oil form, particularly to children — an issue for the oil, not for burning leaf.
